newsitem.title: USA: Florida tax cap group pleads case to Supreme Court.
newsitem.headline: Florida tax cap group pleads case to Supreme Court.

text.p: Fresh from a landslide victory in November, tax limitation backers took more proposals to the Florida Supreme Court Monday in a quest to wrest tax control from the hands of state and local lawmakers.

Three proposed constitutional amendments severely limiting elected governments' ability to create or raise taxes were presented to the state's highest court by the TaxCap Committee, an Orlando-based group attempting to put the issues before Florida voters in 1998.

TaxCap supporters said the three amendments would "return taxing power to ordinary citizens." TaxCap attorney Joe Littlesaid government officials have squandered taxpayers' money and cannot be trusted.

Opponents, including local, regional and state governing organizations, told the court that the measures would impair the ability of governing bodies to do their jobs because they could be precluded from increasing taxes to meet increasing demands for services.
The first measure presented Monday would require voter approval of all new taxes, all tax increases and the repeal of any tax exemption.

It would allow taxing authorities, such as school boards, cities, county commissions, or water management districts, to levy taxes on a 12-month emergency basis if needed to prevent a threat to public health and safety.
Backers said the measure compliments the TaxCap initiative approved by voters in November, which requires two-thirds voter approval for new statewide taxes and tax hikes.
Opponents said the combination would be disasterous and would further hamstring local governments already facing tough finanical decisions.

"What this amendment really does is to attempt destroy representative government in all matters of taxation," said attorney Bob Nabors, who argued against the proposal on behalf of the state. "At risk are all the fundamental guarantees of the (state) constitution."
The second TaxCap proposal would require governing bodies to pay full compensation to property owners whose holdings decrease in value because of a government restriction.
The third proposed amendment is mainly technical and would allow petition initiatives to address more than one subject when dealing with homeowner compensation issues.

The state supreme court is required under the Florida Constitution to review ballot proposals deals to ensure taht they are clearly worded and not misleading, and that they address a single subject. Petition backers must still collect nearly 429,000 certifies signatures to put the proposals on the 1998 ballot. Given TaxCap's statewide organization and track record, the group is expected to have little trouble in soliciting signatures.
